scan.summary: This is your company's written Emergency Action Plan for the Portland facility, last revised in February 2021. In Oregon it is governed by Oregon OSHA's rule OAR 437-002-0042. It covers alarms, evacuation, shelter-in-place, headcounts, first aid and training well. However, it leaves out several things the rule requires: how to report an emergency, how to shut down critical equipment, and who to contact about the plan. It also doesn't say what to do about a chemical spill inside the building, and there is no sign it has been reviewed since 2021.
scan.freshness_note: The plan says only 'Revised February 2021', so the day of the month is a placeholder. That makes it about five years and seven months old. Section 6 promises a review by the facilities lead every January, which would mean five reviews (2022 through 2026), but nothing in the file shows any of them happened. Ask the facilities lead whether a newer version or a review record exists. If not, this plan needs to be revised now.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan says what the alarm sounds like and that manual pull stations are at each exit. It never says who calls 911 or the fire department, how, or from where. It also doesn't say how to report a chemical release or medical emergency. It says emergency medical services 'are called' but not by whom.
gaps.fix: Add a short reporting step: pull the nearest station, call 911 from a safe place, and tell the incident coordinator (by job title). Say who confirms that the alarm monitoring company has sent the fire department.
gaps.locator: Should sit in Section 2 or Section 3; not in the document
gaps.quote: Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor first aid.

gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
gaps.description: The plan tells employees to 'secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds.' It names no equipment that must be shut down before evacuating, such as transfer pumps, lab fume hoods or heat sources, dispensing lines, forklift charging, or process gas. It doesn't say who stays behind to do it. The only shutdown mentioned is the ventilation during shelter-in-place.
gaps.fix: List the critical equipment in the warehouse, lab and loading dock. Assign each item to a job title, with the shutdown step and the point at which that person must leave anyway. If nothing needs shutting down, say so in writing.
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit

gaps.title: Incident coordinator role never assigned
gaps.description: Section 4 relies on an 'incident coordinator' to receive the headcount, brief the fire department and give the all-clear. The plan never says who that is, what their job title is, or who stands in on another shift.
gaps.fix: Name the incident coordinator by job title, with a backup for each shift, and add the role to the Appendix B roster.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(b) (procedures to account for all employees). This is my reading of the rule.
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: No names or job titles of people to contact about the plan
gaps.description: The plan doesn't name anyone employees can go to for more information about the plan or their duties under it. 'Facilities lead' appears, but only as the person who tests alarms and reviews the plan, not as a contact.
gaps.fix: Add a contact line giving the name or job title (and phone or extension) of the plan owner and a backup.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2), matching 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6) in the federal rule. I confirmed subsections (a) through (d) of the Oregon rule but not the exact letter for this element.

gaps.title: No instructions for a chemical spill or release inside the building
gaps.description: The plan covers an outdoor chemical release (shelter in place) and exposure of a person (shower and eyewash). It doesn't say what employees do when a container leaks or spills inside the warehouse or lab. It doesn't say who may clean up an incidental spill, when to evacuate instead, or that employees don't respond to large releases. For a chemical distributor, this is the most likely emergency.
gaps.fix: Add a section on indoor spills and releases. Say which small spills trained staff may clean up, with the spill kit and PPE, and when to evacuate and call 911. If employees are not to respond to releases, say that plainly. The HAZWOPER emergency-response plan requirement generally does not apply to employers who evacuate everyone and don't respond, as long as the plan covers the release.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1) and (q)(2). I believe Oregon adopts this by reference in Division 2, Subdivision H, but I did not check the Oregon adoption.
gaps.locator: Should sit after Section 3; not in the document
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not in the file
gaps.description: The exit route assignments depend on the evacuation maps (Appendix A). The wardens and first-aid responders are named only on the roster (Appendix B). Neither appendix is attached. The plan ends with the appendix titles only.
gaps.fix: Attach the current evacuation maps and a dated roster, and check that they match what is posted at each exit door.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) (procedures for emergency evacuation, including exit route assignments)
gaps.quote: Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)

gaps.title: Silent on who may use fire extinguishers
gaps.description: The plan never says whether employees are expected to fight small fires with portable extinguishers or to evacuate without trying. Which Oregon OSHA extinguisher training duties apply depends on that choice.
gaps.fix: State the policy: either no employee fights fires, or named or trained employees may use extinguishers on small fires. Then line up the matching training.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0187 (portable fire extinguishers). I did not confirm the exact subsection.

gaps.title: No record that the promised January reviews happened
gaps.description: Section 6 commits the facilities lead to review the plan every January. The plan is still marked February 2021, with no review log or sign-off for any year since.
gaps.fix: Hold the review now. Add a review log (date, reviewer, changes) to the plan, and keep records of drills and warden and responder training alongside it.
gaps.citation: The plan's own commitment in Section 6. No specific rule citation.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January

gaps.title: Earthquake named in scope but no earthquake procedure
gaps.description: Section 1 lists earthquakes as an emergency the plan covers. No section says what to do during or after shaking, such as drop, cover and hold on. It also doesn't say to stay away from racking and chemical storage, or when to evacuate and check for spills afterwards. The alarm-driven evacuation steps don't fit an earthquake.
gaps.fix: Add a short earthquake section covering the warehouse racks and the lab, and what happens after the shaking stops: evacuate, take a headcount, and check for leaks before anyone goes back in.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) (procedures for emergency evacuation, including type of evacuation). This is my reading. The rule doesn't mention earthquakes by name.
gaps.locator: Section 1 names it; no procedure section
gaps.quote: when there is a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility

deadlines.source_line: Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually.

deadlines.title: Annual plan review by the facilities lead (next: January 2027; reviews for 2022–2026 not evidenced)
deadlines.source_line: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

facts.quote: It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility
facts.affects: More than 10 employees means the plan must be written (OAR 437-002-0042(1)(b)). The headcount also drives other size thresholds.

facts.value: Warehouse, delivery drivers, laboratory and office staff at the Portland facility
facts.quote: including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff
facts.affects: A laboratory may bring in the lab chemical hygiene standard. Drivers moving chemicals may bring in DOT hazmat training.

facts.value: Monitored fire alarm with horns and strobes, watched 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract, with manual pull stations at each exit
facts.quote: The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract.
facts.affects: Covers the alarm system element. Expect a service contract and test and inspection records.

facts.value: Emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock
facts.quote: taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock
facts.affects: Shows where the eyewash and shower are. Whether there are enough, placed close enough to the lab and other corrosive-handling areas, isn't shown.

facts.value: The site runs more than one shift
facts.quote: trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster)
facts.affects: Wardens, first-aid responders and the incident coordinator must be covered on every shift.

scan.confidence_notes: The file read cleanly, all five pages. I took the title, issuer, site and revision date from page 1, and the 42-employee count and operations from Section 1 on page 2. The revision date says only 'February 2021', so the 2021-02-01 day is a placeholder. I checked the Oregon rule text for OAR 437-002-0042(1)(b) and (2)(a) through (d). I'm confident about the missing reporting procedure and the missing equipment shutdown procedure. I did not confirm the Oregon subsection letter for the contact-person element, the Oregon adoption of HAZWOPER (q), or the extinguisher subsection. Those citations are marked as unconfirmed. The indoor spill, extinguisher and earthquake findings are my judgement of what this plan needs, not word-for-word rule requirements. I haven't seen Appendices A and B, so I can't say whether the exit route assignments and roster are complete or up to date. That multiple shifts are run is my inference from 'two per shift'.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
